title: A Child Promised to a Barren Woman
sum: Israel falls back into evil, and the LORD hands it over to the Philistines for forty years. This time no one cries out for help. Instead, the angel of the LORD comes unasked to the barren wife of Manoah, a Danite of Zorah, and promises a son. The boy will be God's Nazirite from the womb: no razor is to touch his head, and he will begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines. The mother herself must avoid wine and unclean food.

Manoah prays to hear the message for himself, but the angel comes back to his wife and only repeats what she already knows. When Manoah offers a meal, the visitor turns it into a burnt offering and rises to heaven in its flame. Manoah fears they will die for seeing God; his wife reasons that God would not have accepted their gift if he meant to kill them. The child is born and named Samson, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him.
readings: Read as a birth announcement

The chapter follows the pattern of Isaac, Samuel and John the Baptist: a barren woman, a heavenly messenger, a promised son with a special calling. The pattern raises hopes that this child will be a great deliverer. The rest of Samson's story will test those hopes.
Read as a story about seeing

The wife sees and understands; the husband asks and doubts. The angel will not give his name, which is "wonderful," but shows who he is by going up in the fire. The chapter is about who perceives God rightly, a theme that turns grim when Samson, who follows his eyes, loses them.

views.H: Manoah's family lived in Zorah when the Philistines dominated the Shephelah, the 1100s or 1000s BC. A real angelic visit announced a real Nazirite child.
views.C: Most critical scholars see an old hero legend of the Danite clan, framed by the editor's cycle (13:1) and shaped on the pattern of other birth stories. Some think the Nazirite theme was added to explain the hero's long hair.
views.L: Literary readers note that the chapter breaks the book's cycle (no crying out), gives the wife the leading role, and plants details that return: the razor, the vineyard, "to his dying day."
views.J: The rabbis honor Manoah's wife and name her Hazzelelponi (Bava Batra 91a). The Mishnah speaks of a "Samson-Nazirite," a lifelong vow that forbids cutting the hair but not contact with the dead (Nazir 1:2).
views.X: Christians have often seen the angel of the LORD, whose name is "wonderful," as the Son of God before his birth, and Samson's birth as a forerunner of the births of John the Baptist and of Jesus (Luke 1).

deep.b:
Numbers 6 describes a voluntary vow by a man or a woman for a set time: no grape products, no razor, no contact with the dead. At the end, the hair is shaved and burned with a peace offering (Numbers 6:13–18). Samson's case is different. God imposes it before birth; it lasts his whole life; and the angel's words focus on the razor. The mother keeps the food rules while she carries him.

This explains why readers disagree on whether Samson broke his vow when he touched a dead lion or held a drinking feast (14:8–10). If the full Numbers 6 rules applied, he broke them early and often. If his was a special "Samson-Nazirite" vow, as the Mishnah holds, only the hair mattered, and his fall in chapter 16 is the one true breach. Either way, the story makes the hair the sign of his bond to God.

Manoah asks the visitor's name so they can honor him. The answer, "It is wonderful, beyond grasping," echoes Jacob's night at the Jabbok ("Why is it that you ask my name?" Genesis 32:29). In both stories, God's messenger keeps his name hidden and leaves a blessing. Isaiah later gives the promised royal child the title Pele' Yo'ets, "Wonderful Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6), using the same root. Jewish readers have usually understood an angel guarding God's mystery. Many Christian readers have seen the Son of God. A third view takes "wonderful" not as a name at all but as a refusal: the name is too wonderful to tell.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the wife's two omissions
deep.b: This is my own reading. When the woman reports the angel's message (13:7), she leaves out two things: the razor and the promise that her son will rescue Israel. Those are exactly the two things Samson will lose: his hair (16:19), and with it the chance to finish what he began. What she adds, "to his dying day," is fulfilled in 16:30. The chapter may be telling us, through what a mother remembered, which parts of the promise would hold and which would be broken. Alter and Exum note the changes in her retelling; I am pushing their observation further than they do.

echoes: Genesis 18:1–15; Genesis 32:24–30; Numbers 6:1–21; 6:11–24; 1 Samuel 1:1–28; Isaiah 9:6; Luke 1:5–25; Luke 1:26–38

settings.what: The angel's promise to Manoah's wife
settings.by: The angel of the LORD
settings.to: The barren wife of Manoah, a Danite of Zorah
settings.when: during forty years under the Philistines, when no one cried out
settings.why: The angel promises a son who will be God's Nazirite from the womb and will begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines. The mother herself must avoid wine and unclean food. This time God acts without being asked. The rules of the Nazirite (Numbers 6) set up the whole Samson story.

settings.what: Manoah's prayer and the angel's return
settings.by: Manoah, his wife and the angel
settings.to: The LORD; then the angel, and each other
settings.why: Manoah prays to hear the message himself, but the angel repeats what his wife already knew. The visitor goes up in the flame of the offering, and Manoah fears they will die. His wife reasons that God would not have accepted their gift if he meant to kill them. The story shows the unnamed woman as the wiser of the two.

traditions.q: Was the angel of the LORD the Son of God before he became man?
views: Yes. Justin Martyr and many early fathers taught that the one who appeared as the angel of the LORD was the Word, the Son of God (Dialogue with Trypho 56–62). Orthodox theologians still read these appearances this way, and some question Augustine's different view (Bogdan Bucur).

The Church has not ruled on it. Augustine argued that God usually appeared through created angels who spoke in his name, since the Son became visible only at his birth (On the Trinity, books 2–3), and much of later Western theology followed him.

Calvin wrote that the chief angel in these stories was the eternal Word, already acting as mediator (Institutes 1.13.10). Many Reformed and evangelical teachers call such scenes Christophanies, appearances of Christ.

title: A Lion, a Riddle and a Wedding
sum: Samson sees a Philistine woman at Timnah and demands that his parents get her for him, because she is right in his eyes. The narrator adds that this was from the LORD, who was seeking a pretext against the Philistines. On the way, the Spirit of the LORD sweeps down on Samson and he tears apart a lion with his bare hands. Later he finds bees and honey in its carcass, eats, and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from.

At the wedding feast Samson poses a riddle to thirty Philistine companions: "Out of the eater, food came out." Unable to solve it, they threaten to burn his bride and her family unless she gets the answer. She weeps until he tells her, and she tells them. Samson pays his bet by killing thirty men in Ashkelon and taking their clothes, then storms home. His bride is given to his best man.
readings: Read as God's hidden plan

Samson's desire is self-centered, but God works through it to start the conflict with the Philistines that Israel itself would not start. The chapter teaches providence: God can use even a flawed man's choices.
Read as a character study

Samson is led by his eyes and appetites. He ignores his parents, touches the dead, hosts a drinking feast, hides the truth, and repays a lost bet with murder. The Spirit's power does not change his character.
Read through the bride's eyes

Feminist readers note that the unnamed bride is threatened by her own people, distrusted by her husband, blamed for the leak, and handed to another man. She is the first of several women in Judges 13–21 caught between men's conflicts.

views.H: A real marriage across a hostile border, set at Timnah (Tel Batash). The killings at Ashkelon began Samson's private war against Philistine rule.
views.C: Critical scholars often classify the Samson stories as folk tales of a trickster and strongman, close to tales about Heracles, given a theological frame by 14:4 and the Spirit formula.
views.L: The chapter sets up patterns that repeat in chapter 16: a woman "lures" Samson with tears and nagging, he gives in on the seventh day, and violence follows. The verb "go down" begins Samson's long descent.
views.J: The rabbis link Samson's eyes with his fate (Mishnah Sotah 1:8) and debate whether his marriage was permitted. Most read it as the start of his downfall.
views.X: Christian commentators have read 14:4 as a lesson in providence. Early Christian allegory found Christ in the story, for instance reading the honey taken from the lion as sweetness won from a defeated enemy.

deep.b: Samson's riddle is unsolvable to anyone who did not see the lion, which makes it a trick rather than a fair puzzle. The Philistines' answer, "What is sweeter than honey? / What is stronger than a lion?" (14:18), is clever in its own way: it is phrased as another riddle. Some scholars have proposed that the answer to their question would be "love," making their reply a sly comment on how they learned the secret. Samson's retort about plowing with his heifer shows he knows exactly how. The scene ends in violence because riddles in this story are contests of honor, and Samson cannot bear to lose.

Samson never leads an army, never gathers the tribes, and never frees Israel. His fights are personal. Yet the book says twice that he "judged Israel" (15:20; 16:31), the Spirit empowers him four times, and Hebrews 11:32 counts him among the heroes of faith. Readers have weighed this tension in many ways. Some see God working through a lone fighter when Israel would not fight. Others see the book's decline reaching its lowest point in a judge who acts only for himself. Most see both.

echoes: Genesis 24:3–4; Genesis 34:4; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; 1 Samuel 17:34–36; Proverbs 1:6; 1 Kings 10:1; John 3:29; Hebrews 11:32

settings.by: Samson, and his father and mother
settings.to: His parents; then Samson
settings.when: after he sees a woman in Timnah
settings.why: Samson tells his parents to get him the Philistine woman. They object: is there no woman among their own people, that he must marry one of the uncircumcised? He insists, because she is right in his eyes. The narrator then says this was from the LORD, who was seeking a pretext against the Philistines (14:4). Readers see God at work even through a willful hero.

settings.by: Samson, and the Philistine companions in answer
settings.to: Thirty Philistine companions at his wedding feast in Timnah
settings.when: during the seven days of the feast
settings.why: "Out of the eater, food came out" refers to the honey in the lion's body, which no one else saw. The Philistines get the answer by threatening the bride. The riddle starts the fight between Samson and the Philistines, which the narrator says the LORD was seeking (14:4).

title: Foxes, Fire and a Donkey's Jawbone
sum: Samson returns to Timnah to claim his wife and learns she has been given to his best man. In revenge he ties three hundred foxes tail to tail with torches and burns the Philistines' grain, vineyards and olive groves. The Philistines retaliate by burning his wife and her father. Samson slaughters them and hides in the rock of Etam.

The Philistines move into Judah. Rather than fight, three thousand men of Judah come to tie Samson up and hand him over. He lets them. At Lehi, as the Philistines shout, the Spirit of the LORD sweeps down on him, the ropes fall away, and with the jawbone of a donkey he kills a thousand men. Then, dying of thirst, he prays for the first time, and God splits open a hollow at Lehi so that water flows. The chapter closes: Samson judged Israel twenty years.
readings: Read as an escalating feud

Every act in this chapter is justified as paying back the last one. The story shows how revenge grows until whole fields and families are destroyed, and only God's gift of water ends the scene in something other than blood.
Read as the abandoned deliverer

Judah, which led the conquest in chapter 1, now serves the Philistines and hands over the one man fighting them. The deliverer is alone, bound by his own people, and saved only by the Spirit of the LORD.

views.H: These events happened in the Shephelah on the Judah-Philistia border. Lehi and En-hakkore were known places when the book was written ("to this day").
views.C: Many critical scholars see local legends explaining place names (Ramath-lehi, En-hakkore) gathered around the hero. 15:20 looks like the original ending of a shorter Samson cycle.
views.L: The chapter balances fire and water, revenge and rescue. Samson's first prayer comes at his weakest moment, a pattern repeated at his death (16:28).
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers Samson as a judge despite his faults; the Talmud says he judged Israel "like their Father in heaven" for twenty years, seeing his sole fight against Philistia as service to God.
views.X: Christian readers have seen Judah's betrayal of Samson as a type of Jesus handed over by his own people, and the water from the hollow as God's provision, like the water from the rock (Exodus 17; 1 Corinthians 10:4).

deep.b: The men of Judah ask Samson, "Don't you know the Philistines are our masters?" (15:11). The tribe that was first to fight in 1:1–2 has accepted foreign rule as normal. They bring three thousand men, more than enough to fight the Philistine raiding party, and use them to tie up their own champion. The scene shows how deep the oppression has gone: Israel no longer wants to be rescued. In chapter 20, Judah will again be sent first, this time against Benjamin.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the jawbone and the bone-cutting
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. Samson's greatest victory comes with a fresh bone from a dead animal, unclean flesh (Leviticus 11:39). The book's last war begins with another body cut "bone by bone" (19:29) and sent through Israel. In both stories, a dead body becomes a weapon or a summons, and a man claims it was justice. If the parallel is intended, the book shows Israel moving from a single man's misuse of the dead to a whole nation's. I know of no commentator who links the two passages this way, and the connection may be accidental.

settings.by: Three thousand men of Judah, and Samson
settings.to: Samson in the rock of Etam
settings.when: after the Philistines move into Judah
settings.why: The men of Judah ask, "Don't you know the Philistines are our masters?" They tie him up to hand him over. Judah, which led at the start (1:2), now serves the oppressor. The scene shows how far Israel has fallen.

settings.by: Samson
settings.to: Himself, and all who heard of the deed
settings.when: after killing a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone at Lehi
settings.why: The short chant plays on the Hebrew word for donkey and heap. It boasts in his own strength, with no word of the LORD.

settings.by: Samson
settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: dying of thirst after the battle at Lehi
settings.why: For the first time Samson calls to the LORD and calls himself God's servant. God breaks open the hollow at Lehi, and water pours out. The prayer shows that even this rescuer depends on God.

title: Delilah and the Fall of a Strongman
sum: At Gaza, Samson spends the night with a prostitute, escapes an ambush, and carries the city gates up toward Hebron. Then he loves Delilah in the Sorek Valley. The Philistine rulers offer her a fortune to find the secret of his strength. Three times he gives her a false answer, and three times he breaks free. Worn down by her nagging, he finally tells her the truth: no razor has touched his head, for he is God's Nazirite. She lulls him to sleep and shaves off his braids. His strength is gone, because the LORD has left him.

The Philistines blind him and set him grinding grain in the Gaza prison. But his hair begins to grow. At a great feast to their god Dagon, they bring Samson out to entertain them. He asks the boy leading him to place him by the pillars, prays for strength one last time, and pulls the building down, killing more in his death than in his life.
readings: Read as tragedy

A man gifted beyond all others throws his gift away for a woman who sells him. He loses his eyes, his freedom and his dignity, and finds God again only at the end. Milton's Samson Agonistes reads the story this way.
Read as God's victory

The Philistines praise Dagon for defeating Samson, but the real contest is between Dagon and the LORD. In the end the LORD answers Samson's prayer and brings down Dagon's house, as he will later topple Dagon's statue (1 Samuel 5).
Read as Israel's story
Some scholars (Greenstein, Webb) read Samson as a picture of Israel itself: set apart from birth, drawn to foreign partners, betrayed, blinded and taken captive, yet able to call on God and be heard.

views.H: A real fall and death, set at Gaza in a Philistine temple of a kind now known from excavations at Tell Qasile.
views.C: Critical scholars often see a folk tale of the betrayed strongman whose strength lies in his hair, a motif known in many cultures, turned into a story of a broken vow and God's power.
views.L: Delilah's three tests mirror the wife's seven days in chapter 14. Samson's eyes, his "heart," his hair and his prayers are the threads that tie the story together.
views.J: The Mishnah says Samson went after his eyes, so the Philistines put out his eyes (Sotah 1:8). The rabbis still honor him as a judge, and debate whether his death was a permitted act of war or a sin.
views.X: Hebrews 11:32 lists Samson among the heroes of faith. Augustine defended his death as commanded by the Spirit (City of God 1.21). Medieval Christians saw Samson carrying the gates of Gaza as a picture of the Resurrection, and his death as a faint picture of Christ's, who won his greatest victory by dying.

deep.b: Delilah became the Western symbol of the treacherous woman, painted by Rubens and Rembrandt and sung in Saint-Saëns's opera Samson and Delilah. The Bible is sparer. It never says she was a Philistine, never gives her a family, and never says she loved Samson. Feminist critics such as J. Cheryl Exum argue that the story voices men's fear of women's power, and that Delilah is more a figure of male imagination than a full person. Mieke Bal reads her as a woman who seeks knowledge and is honest about her aims. Traditional readers answer that she betrayed a man who loved her for silver. Each reading takes seriously something the text says, and something it leaves out.

deep.h: Where did Samson's strength come from?
deep.b: Samson tells Delilah that if he is shaved he will be weak (16:17), and many readers have concluded that his power lay in his hair. The narrator's comment says otherwise: "He did not know that the LORD had left him" (16:20). The strength was the Spirit's gift (14:6, 19; 15:14). The uncut hair was the sign of his dedication. When he let the last sign of his vow go, God withdrew. When his hair grows, he does not simply recover; he prays, "Lord GOD, remember me, please!" (16:28), and God answers.

echoes: Numbers 6:5–8; 1 Samuel 5:1–7; 1 Samuel 16:14; 1 Samuel 31:4; Proverbs 7:21–27; Luke 23:42; Hebrews 11:32–34

settings.by: The rulers of the Philistines, Delilah and Samson
settings.to: Delilah; then Samson, in the Sorek Valley
settings.when: after Samson falls in love with Delilah
settings.why: The Philistine rulers offer Delilah eleven hundred pieces of silver each to find the secret of his strength. Four times she asks him. Three times he lies, and three times he breaks free. Worn down, he opens his whole heart: he is God's Nazirite from the womb, and no razor has touched his head (16:17). The talk brings his fall. For readers, it shows the rescuer of Israel giving away for love what God had given him, and Philistine silver buying what Philistine armies could not.

settings.by: The rulers and people of the Philistines
settings.to: Their god Dagon, at a great sacrifice in his temple at Gaza
settings.when: after Samson is captured and blinded
settings.why: They praise Dagon for giving Samson into their hand. The song makes the contest one between gods. Samson's death that follows answers it: Dagon's house falls.

settings.by: Samson
settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: brought out to entertain the Philistines, standing between the pillars
settings.why: Samson asks God to remember him and give him strength once more, for revenge for his two eyes. He asks to die with the Philistines. God answers. The prayer is still about himself, yet it ends his life by beginning Israel's rescue.

title: A Shrine of Stolen Silver
sum: The book's ending begins with a family drama in the hill country of Ephraim. Micah confesses to his mother that he stole her eleven hundred pieces of silver, the same sum each Philistine ruler paid Delilah. She blesses him, dedicates the silver to the LORD, and has part of it made into a carved idol and a cast idol. Micah sets up a house of God with an ephod and household gods and ordains one of his sons as priest. The narrator comments: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes.

A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, wandering to find a place to live, arrives at Micah's house. Micah hires him as father and priest for ten pieces of silver a year, clothes and food. Micah is delighted: now that he has a Levite, the LORD will surely treat him well.
readings: Read as religion gone wrong

Every act in the chapter is done in the LORD's name: a blessing, a dedication, a shrine, a priest. Every one breaks the law. The chapter shows how sincere people can build a religion out of their own wishes.
Read as a case for kingship
The refrain in 17:6 explains the chaos: no king enforced the law of one sanctuary and one priesthood. Read this way, the chapter prepares for a king who will set worship right.

views.H: Micah's shrine was a real local sanctuary that later became the shrine at Dan. The events likely belong early in the judges period.
views.C: Many critical scholars read chapters 17–18 as a polemic against the sanctuary at Dan, which Jeroboam later made a royal shrine (1 Kings 12:29), written to show that it began with stolen silver and a stolen idol.
views.L: The repeated eleven hundred pieces link the chapter to Delilah (16:5). The "house of God" in Ephraim is set against the true house of God at Shiloh (18:31). Micah's name, "Who is like the LORD?", is ironic.
views.J: The rabbis taught that Micah's idol stood within sight of Shiloh, and that Micah was not denied a share in the world to come because he fed travelers (Sanhedrin 103b). Rabbinic chronology dates the story to the generation after Joshua.
views.X: Christian readers see a warning against worship shaped by personal taste and against treating religion as a way to secure blessing. The hired Levite is often compared with the hired hand of John 10:12–13.

deep.b: Four times in five chapters the book says there was no king in Israel (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25), twice adding that everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes. The words recall Deuteronomy 12:8, where Moses warns against "each of us doing whatever is right in his own eyes" in matters of worship. The refrain can be read at least three ways. (1) A plea for monarchy: a godly king would have stopped this. (2) A plea for a particular king: the villains are tied to Saul (Gibeah, Jabesh-gilead, Benjamin), and the victims and sanctuaries to Judah and Bethlehem, David's town. (3) An ironic refrain: kings will fail too, as Kings shows, and the true problem is that Israel has forgotten its divine King (8:23). Each view has strong advocates. Webb and Block lean toward (1), and Brettler and Amit develop (2). Martin Buber saw two books joined together: an anti-king book built on Gideon's refusal (8:23) and Jotham's fable, and a pro-king book, chapters 17–21, to which the refrain belongs. William Dumbrell is among those who argue (3).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the silver that changes hands
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. Eleven hundred pieces of silver appear only twice in the Bible: the bribe each Philistine ruler paid Delilah (16:5) and Micah's mother's stolen silver (17:2). If the sum is meant to link the stories, the effect is to make the money that bought Israel's strongest man the same money that buys a private idol. The silver passes from hand to hand: from a mother's curse to a blessing, to a silversmith, to an idol, to the Danites, to the shrine at Dan. Many commentators note the matching sums (Webb among them); my addition is to read the silver as a single thread binding the book's two halves of failure, the judge who sold his calling and the people who bought their gods.

echoes: Exodus 20:4; Exodus 32:1–6; Deuteronomy 12:8; Deuteronomy 27:15; 8:27; 1 Kings 12:28–31; Genesis 31:19–35

settings.what: A stolen silver and a mother's blessing
settings.by: Micah and his mother
settings.to: Each other
settings.when: when Micah confesses he took her eleven hundred pieces of silver
settings.why: His mother turns her curse into a blessing. She sets the silver apart for the LORD, to make an idol. The words mix the LORD's name with the very thing the law forbids (Exodus 20:4). The narrator's refrain explains why: there was no king, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes (17:6).

settings.by: Micah, and the Levite
settings.to: A young Levite from Bethlehem looking for a place to live; then Micah to himself
settings.when: when the Levite arrives at Micah's house
settings.why: "Be my father and my priest," Micah says, offering ten pieces of silver a year, clothes and keep. The Levite agrees. Then Micah says, "Now I am sure the LORD will treat me well, since I've got a Levite for my priest" (17:13). The words show religion bought as a way to secure blessing. Readers who knew the law see how wrong it is: the shrine, the idol and the hired priest all break it.

title: Dan Takes a Priest and a Town
sum: The tribe of Dan, unable to hold its land, sends five scouts north. At Micah's house they recognize the young Levite and ask him to inquire of God. He tells them their road lies before the LORD. At Laish, near the springs of the Jordan, they find a quiet, defenseless people far from any ally, and they report that the land is excellent.

Six hundred armed Danites march north. At Micah's house they take his idol, ephod and household gods, and invite the Levite to be priest to a whole tribe. He gladly goes. When Micah chases them, crying "My gods that I made, you've taken them," they threaten his life. The Danites burn Laish, rebuild it as Dan, and set up Micah's idol, with Jonathan, grandson of Moses, and his descendants as priests until the exile.
readings: Read as a parody of conquest

Spies, a good report, an armed march and a captured city: the chapter follows the pattern of Numbers 13 and Joshua 2 and 7. But the spies consult a hired priest, the victims are peaceful, and the prize is a stolen idol. The conquest is acted out without God.
Read as the origin of Dan's shrine

Dan became one of the two royal sanctuaries of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29). This chapter tells how the shrine began: with stolen silver, a stolen idol and a priest for hire. Readers in Judah would hear it as an exposé.

views.H: The Danites really did migrate north, as Joshua 19:47 also reports. Tel Dan's excavations show a new settlement in the Iron Age on the ruins of the older city of Laish.
views.C: Critical scholars generally see an anti-Dan, and so anti-northern, polemic written in Judah, perhaps after the fall of the north (18:30). Some think the priestly line from Moses was an authentic claim of Dan's priests that the story turns against them.
views.L: The chapter echoes the conquest and the patriarchs (Laban's stolen gods), mocks a god who can be carried off, and lets the victims of Laish keep the narrator's sympathy.
views.J: The Talmud says Jonathan was Moses' grandson, linked to Manasseh because he acted like Manasseh (Bava Batra 109b); Rashi adds that the raised letter in 18:30 was written out of respect for Moses. Some rabbis identify Jonathan with Shebuel, who later repented and served in David's treasury (1 Chronicles 26:24).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the Levite a warning against religious leaders who follow money and influence, and in Micah's cry a picture of all who trust in gods they have made.

deep.h: The Danite migration in the Bible
deep.b: Dan's story is told in three places. Joshua 19:40–48 lists Dan's towns near the coast and adds in one verse that the territory "slipped out of their hands," so they took Leshem and renamed it Dan. Judges 1:34 says the Amorites pushed the Danites into the hills. Judges 18 gives the full story. Later, Dan became the northern edge of Israel ("from Dan to Beersheba"), the site of Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kings 12:29), and the first area taken into exile by Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Dan is missing from the list of tribes in Revelation 7:5–8, and some early Christian writers, such as Irenaeus, connected that absence with a belief that the Antichrist would come from Dan.

The scouts speak the language of the promise: "God has given it into your hand" (18:10). Laish lay within the northern limits God had promised (Numbers 34:7–9), so some traditional readers defend the move. But the law commanded Israel to offer peace to distant towns (Deuteronomy 20:10), the oracle came from a hired priest, and the narrator stresses twice that Laish was calm and unsuspecting (18:7, 27). Most readers, ancient and modern, conclude that the chapter presents a land grab dressed as holy war.

echoes: Joshua 19:40–48; Numbers 13:1–33; Joshua 2:1–24; Genesis 31:19–35; Deuteronomy 20:10–15; 1 Kings 12:28–31; 2 Kings 15:29; Revelation 7:4–8

settings.what: The Levite's oracle for the Danites
settings.by: Five Danite scouts, and the Levite in answer
settings.to: The Levite at Micah's house
settings.why: The Levite tells them their road "lies before the LORD," a vague word from a hired priest at an illegal shrine. The story shows how God's name was used to bless a raid.

settings.by: The five Danite scouts
settings.to: Their tribe at Zorah and Eshtaol
settings.why: They urge the tribe to attack a quiet and safe people. Unlike the scouts sent by Moses and Joshua, they find not a promised land but an easy target.

settings.what: The Danites take the priest, and Micah's cry
settings.by: The Danites, the Levite and Micah
settings.to: The Levite; then Micah
settings.why: They offer the Levite a whole tribe instead of one household, and he goes gladly. Micah cries, "My gods that I made, you've taken them." The words show the emptiness of gods that can be stolen.

title: The Night at Gibeah
sum: A Levite from Ephraim takes a concubine from Bethlehem. She leaves him and returns to her father, and four months later he goes to win her back. Her father detains him with five days of feasting. Leaving late, the Levite refuses to stop in Jebusite Jerusalem, a town of foreigners, and presses on to Gibeah in Benjamin. No one takes them in until an old man, himself an outsider from Ephraim, offers his home.

That night the men of the town surround the house and demand the guest, as the men of Sodom did. The host offers his virgin daughter and the concubine instead. The Levite pushes his concubine out to them, and they rape and abuse her all night. At dawn she collapses at the door with her hands on the threshold. In the morning her husband tells her to get up; she does not answer. He takes her home, cuts her body into twelve pieces, and sends them through Israel. All who see it say nothing like this has happened since the Exodus.
readings: Read as Israel become Sodom
The chapter retells Genesis 19 with Israelites as the men of Sodom. There are no angels to rescue anyone. The point is moral and national: God's people have become what God destroyed.
Read as a text of terror

Phyllis Trible's famous reading follows the woman: unnamed, silent, passed between father, husband, host and mob, and finally cut apart. The narrator does not comment, and Trible asks readers to remember her and to say "never again."
Read as a political story
Gibeah would become Saul's capital. Some scholars read the chapter as part of a case for David's house (from Bethlehem) against Saul's (from Gibeah), told when that rivalry still mattered.

views.H: A real atrocity early in the judges period (Phinehas is still alive in 20:28), remembered for centuries as "the days of Gibeah" (Hosea 9:9; 10:9).
views.C: Many critical scholars see a story shaped by Genesis 19 and by later politics, perhaps written in the monarchy or exile, using an old tradition of a war against Benjamin.
views.L: Literary readers trace how the men speak and the woman never does, how "husband" becomes "master," and how hospitality goes from excess in Bethlehem to none in Gibeah.
views.J: The Talmud blames the Levite's harshness for the quarrel (Gittin 6b) and draws a lesson against frightening one's household. Hosea's "days of Gibeah" made the story a byword in Jewish memory.
views.X: Christian commentators have read the chapter as a picture of human depravity without a king, preparing for the need of a righteous ruler. Some modern Christian writers read the woman's suffering alongside the suffering of Christ, who was also handed over, abused at night and broken.

deep.b:
Traditional readings have usually focused on the crime of the men of Gibeah and on Israel's collective guilt. Commentators such as Block are severe on every man in the story: the father who delays, the host who offers the women, and above all the Levite, whom Block judges harshly. The traditional emphasis is that this is what happens when Israel forgets God and there is no just authority.

The older reading that blamed the woman deserves to be stated at its strongest. The Hebrew of 19:2 says she "played the harlot against him," and the KJV translates it so ("played the whore"). Keil and Delitzsch took it as real unfaithfulness, and Pseudo-Philo says she was handed over to the men of Gibeah because she had sinned (Biblical Antiquities 45:3). Its case is simple: this is the received Hebrew text, the Aramaic Targum also reads it as a fault on her side, and the narrator never withdraws the charge. Those who reject this reading answer that both Greek text forms say she became angry or simply left, that a woman guilty of adultery would hardly run to her father's house, that her husband comes "to speak to her heart" (19:3) rather than to accuse her, and that nothing in the story suggests what happened to her was deserved.

Feminist readings ask what the story means for the woman, and for women readers. Phyllis Trible (Texts of Terror, 1984) reads it as one of four biblical stories of terror against women and refuses to let the woman's silence be forgotten. J. Cheryl Exum (Fragmented Women, 1993) argues that the narrative itself, by punishing a woman who left her husband, takes part in the violence it describes. Mieke Bal (Death and Dissymmetry, 1988) reads the whole book's ending through the bodies of its unnamed daughters. Womanist readers, such as Koala Jones-Warsaw, ask readers to see the violence done to the whole community, men and women, and not only to one woman. These approaches disagree with each other in places, but all insist that the woman's story, not only the men's war, is the center of the text.

The two kinds of reading are not opposites. Both see the chapter as an indictment. They differ on whether the text itself condemns everything it shows, or whether readers must supply the condemnation the narrator leaves out.

deep.h: Genesis 19 and Judges 19 side by side
deep.b: Arrival at evening; a host who is himself an outsider; men of the city surrounding the house; the demand to "know" the guest; the host's plea, "my brothers, do not do evil"; the offer of two women; the words "whatever looks good to you." The likenesses are too many to be chance, and most scholars think Judges 19 was told with Genesis 19 in mind. Not all: Susan Niditch (1982) argued that the Judges version is the more original and better fitted to its setting, and that Genesis 19 borrows from it or from a shared tradition. The differences are the message: in Sodom the guests are angels who rescue their host; in Gibeah the guest saves himself by giving up his wife. Sodom is destroyed by God; Gibeah is destroyed by Israel.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a body cut in twelve, a nation cut apart
deep.b: This is my own reading, building on Gale Yee and others who read the woman's body as a symbol of Israel. The Levite cuts his concubine into twelve pieces and sends them to the twelve tribes to call them together. The war that follows cuts one of the twelve off (21:3, 6, 15). What was done to her body is then done to the nation's body: the act meant to unite Israel dismembers it. The book's last chapter is spent trying to sew the twelfth piece back on, and the stitching is made of more stolen women. If this reading holds, the narrator is saying that Israel's response repeated the crime it set out to punish.

echoes: Genesis 19:1–11; Genesis 22:6–10; Genesis 34:1–31; 2 Samuel 13:1–22; 1 Samuel 11:7; Hosea 9:9; Hosea 10:9

settings.what: The men of Gibeah and the old man
settings.by: The men of Gibeah, the old Ephraimite host, and the Levite
settings.to: The old man, the master of the house; then the men of the town; then the concubine
settings.when: at night, while the Levite and his concubine are guests in Gibeah of Benjamin
settings.why: The men of the town pound on the door and demand the guest, to know him. The old man begs them not to do this disgraceful thing. Instead he offers his virgin daughter and the concubine. The words echo Lot at Sodom almost line for line (Genesis 19:5–8). Now the Sodom is an Israelite town. The Levite pushes his concubine out, and at dawn he tells her to get up. When he sends her body through Israel, all who see it say nothing like this has happened since the exodus. For readers, this is what Israel became with no king.
views: In the Hebrew, all who see the body speak. The longer Greek text has the Levite tell his messengers what to say to every Israelite.

title: Civil War against Benjamin
sum: All Israel gathers at Mizpah "like one man," four hundred thousand strong. The Levite tells his version of the night at Gibeah, leaving out his own part. The tribes vow not to go home until Gibeah is punished and demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men. Benjamin refuses and musters for war, including seven hundred left-handed slingers.

Israel asks God who should go first, and the answer is Judah, as in 1:2. Twice Israel attacks, and twice it is beaten, losing forty thousand men. After weeping, fasting and sacrifices at Bethel, where the ark and Phinehas are, God promises victory. On the third day Israel uses an ambush like the one at Ai. Gibeah burns like a whole offering, Benjamin breaks, and twenty-five thousand Benjaminites die. Only six hundred escape to the Rock of Rimmon. Israel then burns every Benjaminite town, people and animals alike.
readings: Read as justice
Israel rightly demands that the guilty be handed over, and God sends them to punish Benjamin when it refuses. The defeats humble Israel too, and the final victory is the LORD's (20:35).
Read as justice gone wild

The demand for a few guilty men becomes the destruction of a tribe, its towns, women and animals. Israel turns the methods of the conquest (the ambush of Ai, the ban) on its own brothers. The story shows how righteous anger can become a second atrocity.

views.H: A real civil war early in the judges period, attested by its lasting effects: Benjamin remained the smallest tribe (1 Samuel 9:21).
views.C: Critical scholars note signs of two accounts combined (20:29–36 and 20:36–48) and huge numbers. Many see a story shaped in Judah to discredit Benjamin and Saul.
views.L: "Like one man" unity, the question of 1:1 asked again, the ambush of Ai repeated: the chapter turns the book's beginning and the conquest upside down.
views.J: The Talmud asks why Israel lost twice at God's word and answers that they were zealous for the concubine's honor but silent about Micah's idol, an offense to God (Sanhedrin 103b); Pseudo-Philo tells it the same way. Benjamin's later restoration is celebrated on the 15th of Av (Bavli Taanit 30b).
views.X: Christian commentators stress the need to seek God's will humbly before acting, not after. Many see the war as a picture of the church's call to discipline sin without destroying the sinner (1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 6:1).

deep.h: Why did God let Israel lose?
deep.b: Twice the LORD says "go up," and twice Israel is cut down. Readers have answered in several ways. (1) Israel asked only who should lead, not whether they should fight; their first questions assumed their own plan. (2) The whole nation shared the guilt of a society in which Gibeah could happen, and needed to be humbled before it could judge. Only after the second defeat do they fast and offer sacrifices (20:26). (3) God was judging both sides: Benjamin for protecting the guilty, Israel for its idolatry (chapters 17–18) and its pride. The text gives no explanation, which leaves the question with the reader.

Israel's methods in this chapter come from the conquest: the ambush (Joshua 8), a burning town "like a whole offering" (Deuteronomy 13:16), and the killing of everything that breathes (Deuteronomy 20:16). Susan Niditch and others see the narrator showing what happens when the ideology of the ban is aimed at fellow Israelites. Traditional commentators agree that Israel exceeded God's command, since nothing in the oracles authorized wiping out the tribe's towns, women and children. The next chapter shows Israel weeping over a result it chose.

echoes: 1:1–2; Joshua 8:1–29; Joshua 22:10–34; Deuteronomy 13:12–18; Deuteronomy 20:16–17; Hosea 10:9; 1 Samuel 11:7

settings.by: The Levite, husband of the murdered woman
settings.to: All Israel gathered at Mizpah, four hundred thousand armed men
settings.why: The Levite tells his version: the men of Gibeah meant to kill him and raped his concubine until she died. He leaves out that he pushed her out himself. The speech shows how one man's account moves a nation to war. Readers who have read chapter 19 know what he does not say.

settings.what: Israel's vow and its demand on Benjamin
settings.by: The Israelites gathered at Mizpah
settings.to: One another; then the tribe of Benjamin
settings.why: The tribes vow not to go home until Gibeah is punished. They demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men, to sweep the evil out of Israel, in the language of Deuteronomy. Benjamin refuses, and civil war follows.

settings.what: Israel asks the LORD three times
settings.by: The Israelites, and the LORD in answer
settings.to: The LORD at Bethel, where the ark and Phinehas were
settings.why: First Israel asks who should go first, and the answer is Judah, as in 1:2. After two defeats they weep and ask again whether to fight their brother. The third time God promises victory. The questions show a people asking God about war only after they have decided on it.

title: Wives for Benjamin
sum: Israel had sworn at Mizpah not to give its daughters to Benjamin. Now, weeping at Bethel, the people ask the LORD why a tribe is missing. They find a way around the oath. No one from Jabesh-gilead came to Mizpah, and another oath demanded death for anyone who stayed away. Twelve thousand men kill the people of Jabesh, sparing four hundred virgins, who are given to Benjamin's six hundred survivors.

Two hundred men still lack wives. The elders tell them to hide in the vineyards at Shiloh during the LORD's yearly festival and seize girls who come out to dance. If fathers or brothers complain, they will be told the oath was not broken, since they did not give their daughters. The Benjaminites do so, rebuild their towns, and the tribes go home. The book ends: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes.
readings: Read as restoration
A tribe nearly lost is saved, the oath is kept, and Benjamin lives to give Israel its first king. Traditional readers often see God preserving all twelve tribes despite Israel's sin.
Read as the final irony

Israel solves the violence of chapter 19 by killing a town and abducting six hundred women. The elders keep their oath on a technicality and break every deeper law. The refrain that closes the book is the narrator's only comment, and it is enough.

views.H: These events explain the later ties between Benjamin and Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11; 31:11–13) and the small size of Benjamin.
views.C: Many critical scholars see two traditions about how Benjamin got wives, joined together, and a political purpose in tying Saul's tribe to violence and abduction.
views.L: The book that began with a daughter given in marriage for a victory (1:12–13) ends with daughters seized at a festival. Literary readers trace how women's fortunes fall across the whole book.
views.J: The Mishnah remembers girls dancing in white in the vineyards on the 15th of Av, and the Talmud says it was the day Benjamin was allowed to marry into Israel again (Taanit 30b). Rabbinic tradition stresses Israel's grief over the lost tribe.
views.X: Christian readers see the book ending in a cry for a righteous king, answered in David and finally in Christ. In Christian Bibles Ruth follows, where a foreign woman is welcomed by kindness in Bethlehem.

deep.h: Women at the end of Judges
deep.b: Judges opens with Achsah, who asks her father for springs of water and gets them (1:12–15), and with Deborah and Jael, who lead and win. As the book goes on, women suffer more and speak less: Jephthah's daughter is sacrificed (11:34–40), Samson's wife is burned (15:6), the Levite's concubine is raped and cut apart (19:25–29), the women of Jabesh are killed and their daughters taken (21:10–12), and the dancers of Shiloh are seized (21:21–23). Susan Ackerman, Mieke Bal, J. Cheryl Exum and others read this downward line as one of the book's main ways of showing Israel's decline. Many traditional commentators agree: the treatment of women is the clearest measure of how far Israel has fallen.

deep.h: How the book ends, and what comes next
deep.b: Judges closes with a refrain rather than a verdict. In the Hebrew canon, 1 Samuel follows, telling of Samuel's birth to a barren woman at Shiloh (the same Shiloh), Israel's demand for a king, and the anointing of Saul the Benjaminite and David of Bethlehem. In Christian Bibles, Ruth comes next, set "In the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). It moves from famine and death to loyalty and new life in Bethlehem, ending with the birth of David's grandfather. Read that way, Ruth answers the dark Bethlehem stories of Judges 17–21 with a story of what Israel could be.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the six hundreds
deep.b: This is my own observation. Six hundred is a recurring number in Judges: Shamgar kills six hundred Philistines (3:31), six hundred Danites march north and seize Laish (18:11), and six hundred Benjaminites survive to seize wives at Shiloh (20:47; 21:23). The two six-hundreds in the book's ending both take what is not theirs and settle down on it. If the echo is meant, the Danites' raid and Benjamin's raid frame the epilogue as twin pictures of a tribe taking by force. The number was also a standard military unit (1 Samuel 13:15; 2 Samuel 15:18), which may be all it means.

echoes: Numbers 31:15–18; 11:30–40; 1 Samuel 1:3; 1 Samuel 11:1–11; 1 Samuel 31:11–13; Ruth 1:1; Deuteronomy 12:8

settings.what: Israel's oaths and its lament for Benjamin
settings.by: The men of Israel
settings.to: The LORD at Bethel, and one another
settings.why: Israel had sworn not to give its daughters to Benjamin. Now it asks the LORD why a tribe is missing, as if God had caused it. The oaths trap them, and they look for a way around them.

settings.by: The community gathered at Mizpah
settings.to: Twelve thousand of its strongest fighters
settings.when: after they find that no one from Jabesh-gilead came to the assembly
settings.why: The community orders the fighters to put Jabesh-gilead to the sword, women and children too. Every male, and every woman who has lain with a man, is to be put under the ban. The order "solves" two problems: the oath of death against anyone who stayed away (21:5), and the lack of wives for Benjamin. The four hundred girls who are spared are given to the Benjaminites. Readers see the ban, meant for Canaan, turned on an Israelite town. Jabesh is the town Saul later rescues (1 Samuel 11).

settings.by: The elders of the community
settings.to: The two hundred Benjaminites still without wives
settings.when: before the yearly festival of the LORD at Shiloh
settings.why: The elders tell the Benjaminites to hide in the vineyards and seize girls who come out to dance. If fathers or brothers complain, they will be told the oath was not broken. The plan keeps the letter of the oath while violating women and a festival of the LORD. The book's last line explains it: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes (21:25).
